html:
The Yoruba are one of the largest peoples of West Africa, living mainly in southwest Nigeria and in neighbouring Benin and Togo. They number some 45 million or more and speak Yoruba, a language of the Niger-Congo family.

Their sacred city is Ife, where they say the world was created and where the first king, Oduduwa, ruled. Ife was a large city by the 1100s, and its artists cast the famous Ife heads in brass and copper. Yoruba life has long centred on walled towns, each with its king, or oba. Earthworks such as Sungbo's Eredo ring old kingdoms.

From the 1600s the cavalry state of Oyo dominated, until it fell apart in the early 1800s under revolt and the push of the Sokoto Caliphate. Long Yoruba wars followed, in which Ibadan rose to power. Many captives were sold into the Atlantic slave trade, which carried Yoruba religion, with its gods called orishas, to Brazil and Cuba, where it lives on in Candomblé and Santería.

The British moved inland from Lagos in the late 1800s. Samuel Ajayi Crowther, a Yoruba freed from a slave ship, became the first African Anglican bishop. In the 1900s prayer churches such as the Celestial Church of Christ grew in Yoruba lands, and Wole Soyinka became Africa's first Nobel laureate in literature.
sum: The Yoruba are one of the largest peoples of West Africa, living mainly in southwest Nigeria and in neighbouring Benin and Togo. They number some 45 million or more and speak Yoruba, a language of the Niger-Congo family.
